passage:
"Is this yours?" Bhupen held out a folded note.
"My lunch money!" Alka had been checking every pocket for ten minutes. "Where was it?"
"Under the bench."
"Thank you, thank you! Take half my sandwich, please."
"No, it's fine. Eat it."
At home Bhupen told Mama, "Alka thanked me three times."
"How did that feel?"
"Really good. But I wish I didn't keep hoping for it. I think I'd have given it back anyway."
"Would you?"
"Yes. I think it would still feel right, only quieter."

qa.q: What does Bhupen feel when Alka thanks him, and what does he tell himself about it?
qa.a: He feels really good, but he tells himself not to keep hoping for thanks each time; he thinks giving it back would still feel right, only quieter.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do if nobody thanks him next time?
qa.a: He can remember that returning the money was right on its own, and let the quiet good feeling be enough.

qa.q: How might Alka have been feeling before Bhupen held out the note?
qa.a: Worried about the lost lunch money, since Alka had been checking every pocket for ten minutes, so the thanks came out of relief.

grounding: Illustrates a child thanked for returning money who learns not to expect a reward every time.
